entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, composed around the 2nd century BCE in ancient India, is a foundational text of Yoga philosophy, attributed to the sage Patanjali. It has played a pivotal role in shaping spiritual practices and the understanding of meditation and mental discipline across various cultures and epochs. The text, composed in Sanskrit, systematically outlines the path to spiritual enlightenment through the eight limbs of yoga, known as Ashtanga, which integrate ethical conduct, physical postures, breath control, and meditative absorption. Its significance extends beyond India, influencing philosophical and spiritual movements worldwide, particularly in the realms of Hinduism and Buddhism.

The Yoga Sutras delineate a comprehensive framework for achieving self-realization and mastery over the mind, addressing the nature of consciousness and the obstacles faced in the pursuit of spiritual growth. Patanjali articulates the concept of 'yoga' as a means of stilling the fluctuations of the mind, offering practical guidance through aphorisms or sutras that are both concise and profound. The text has been commented upon extensively over centuries, influencing yoga practitioners and scholars alike, and has been translated into numerous languages, thus expanding its reach and impact.

The legacy of the Yoga Sutras is profound, as they have shaped not only spiritual practices but also modern psychology and wellness movements. The principles laid out by Patanjali resonate within contemporary yoga practices globally, which often blend physical postures with philosophical teachings. This synthesis has led to a cultural renaissance regarding the appreciation of mindfulness and self-awareness in the West, with yoga evolving into a multi-billion dollar industry. Ultimately, the Yoga Sutras have become a bridge between ancient wisdom and modern existential inquiries, underscoring the timeless pursuit of self-understanding and inner peace.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Yoga Sūtras of Patañjali (Sanskrit: योगसूत्र, Yoga Sūtra) is a foundational text of classical Indian philosophy and the primary systematic exposition of Yoga as a philosophical system, attributed to the sage Patañjali and composed c. 400 CE (with scholarly estimates ranging from c. 200 BCE to c. 400 CE). The text consists of 196 sūtras (aphoristic formulas) divided into four pādas (chapters): Samādhi Pāda (51 sūtras, on the nature and purpose of yoga and its highest stages); Sādhana Pāda (55 sūtras, on the practice of yoga — the Eight Limbs, aṣṭāṅga yoga); Vibhūti Pāda (56 sūtras, on the supernatural powers — siddhis — that arise through practice); and Kaivalya Pāda (34 sūtras, on liberation, kaivalya, and the nature of consciousness).

The Yoga Sūtras define yoga as 'citta-vṛtti-nirodha' ('the cessation of the fluctuations of consciousness') and present the path to liberation through the Eight Limbs (Aṣṭāṅga Yoga): Yama (ethical restraints — non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possessiveness); Niyama (observances — purity, contentment, discipline, study, surrender to the divine); Āsana (posture); Prāṇāyāma (breath control); Pratyāhāra (withdrawal of the senses); Dhāraṇā (concentration); Dhyāna (meditation); and Samādhi (the final state of absorbed concentration and liberation). This system synthesised several earlier Indian philosophical traditions — Sāṃkhya metaphysics (the duality of Puruṣa/consciousness and Prakṛti/matter), Buddhist meditation psychology, and the existing yoga tradition — into the most systematic account of the path to liberation in Hindu thought.
